originalTitle: Why people are dropping out of the workforce and not looking for new jobs: 'The market wore me down'
summary: Candidates giving up in the face of relentless job searches could be part of the reason behind recent declines in the labor force participation rate.
content:
After six months of scouring job listings and sending off resumes, Dan Coda's job search came to an end. He didn't find the technical program or project management job he wanted; he just stopped looking altogether.

Starting around December 2025, when he was laid off from his previous role, Coda says he spent more than 300 hours job hunting, submitting dozens of applications, hearing back about 15 potential roles and going through multiple rounds of interviews to no avail. By June, Coda says he was done with the grueling effort of looking for work.

"The market wore me down," the 40-year-old from Durham, North Carolina, tells CNBC Make It. "I was hitting wall after wall after wall and not getting anywhere."

This year, the number of announced layoffs in January reached a level not seen since 2009, during the Great Recession, according to data from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. "The candidate pool is absolutely flooded," Coda says, citing mass layoffs pushing thousands of affected workers like himself into the job market at once. With that kind of competition, he says, "What chance do you stand?"

Discouraged job seekers like Coda, who have given up on finding work, at least for now, are part of a trend economists say is worrying: The labor force participation rate has been on a downward trajectory since the turn of the millennium, fueled by an aging population and fewer young people entering the workforce.

June saw the biggest one-month drop in prime age labor force participation of workers ages 25 to 54, excluding the Covid-19 pandemic, since June 1976. Roughly 720,000 people stopped working or looking for work between May and June, according to the St. Louis Fed. Those leaving the workforce are both men and women, and the majority are ages 25 to 34, says Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union who specializes in the economics of the middle class.

Meanwhile, elevated levels of long-term unemployment persist. In June, more than 1.9 million Americans, or roughly 1 in 4 unemployed people, were jobless but still looking for work for longer than six months , according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data. A continuous low-hire, low-fire job market could make it more challenging to find work and push more people out of the workforce altogether.

Official numbers on how many people are dropping out of the workforce are likely to be revised downward in the coming months, Long says, noting that the one-month spike indicates "something wasn't quite right" in the initial data pull. But falling labor force participation nonetheless adds to a picture of an American labor economy seemingly out of balance with few solutions in sight.

And the factors pushing people out of the labor force have implications beyond workers paying for everyday essentials, including stunting career trajectories and impacting long-term retirement savings.

Mental health stressors are pushing some people out of the job search: 'I didn't have energy'

Economists say several compounding factors are likely driving down the labor force participation rate, like an exodus of retiring workers and lower immigration into the U.S. Some working parents, especially moms of young kids , and people with disabilities may be striking out as they face more competition for remote or flexible work opportunities that are harder to come by today, Long says.

Mental wellbeing could also play a part. Coda says he stopped his job search in June after a conversation with his wife, who'd noticed how the tiresome process soured his mood.

"Other than the death of a family member or a close friend, [unemployment] is one of the most devastating things that people face," Carl Van Horn, director of the Heldrich Center for Workforce Development at Rutgers University, told CNBC in June.

About half of job seekers say the search negatively impacts their mental health due to rejection, lack of responses, financial pressure and waning motivation, according to an April Resume Genius survey of 1,000 active U.S. job seekers.

Meanwhile, employers also tend to question resume gaps , which can make it harder for candidates to find work the longer they're searching.

Coda says his mental health during his job search, while dispiriting, was less affected by the tepid responses because his family had been saving aggressively. He and his wife, who still works full-time in HR, had been working toward an early retirement. And though they're now dipping into those savings, Coda says the family can better afford his hiatus as they're scaling back on dining out, yard maintenance and housecleaning services.

Others are less lucky. Haina, who like some other people from Inner Mongolia in China has only one name, says she's relying on family after an exhausting job search strained her mental health.

The 33-year-old was living in New York when she was laid off from her marketing analytics role in November 2025. Over the next few months, she set up interviews and even secured a few offers, but she says finding a new employer to accommodate her H-1B visa needs has been difficult. (Employers often have to apply on behalf of employees for visa transfers costing thousands of dollars between filing, processing and attorney fees.)

In May, Haina stopped her U.S.-based job search and headed home to Inner Mongolia to stay with family. Since then, she says she feels more like herself again. The job search was a "roller coaster of ups and downs," Haina says: "If you met me a month ago, I was a completely different person. I didn't have energy."

Haina is currently staying with her parents, which means she has minimal expenses, and says she relishes being home for the first extended period of time since she left for the U.S. eight years ago.

"I just want to really take this [moment] to spend time with my family and really think about what I want to do," she says.

chineseTitle: 为什么人们退出劳动力市场而不是寻找新工作：“市场让我疲惫不堪”
chineseSummary: 候选人在无情的求职面前放弃可能是近期劳动力参与率下降的部分原因。
chineseContent:
经过六个月的搜寻工作列表和发送简历后，丹·科达的求职工作结束了。他没有找到他想要的技术程序或项目管理工作；他完全不再寻找了。

Coda 表示，从 2025 年 12 月左右开始，他从之前的职位被解雇，他花了 300 多个小时寻找工作，提交了数十份申请，收到了大约 15 个潜在职位的回复，并进行了多轮面试，但一无所获。到了六月，科达说他已经不再费力寻找工作了。

“市场让我疲惫不堪，”这位来自北卡罗来纳州达勒姆的 40 岁人士告诉 CNBC Make It。 “我撞了一堵又一堵墙，却一无所获。”

全球就业咨询公司 Challenger, Gray & Christmas 的数据显示，今年 1 月份宣布的裁员数量达到了 2009 年经济大衰退以来的最高水平。科达说：“候选人库已经被淹没了。”他指出，大规模裁员迫使数千名像他这样受到影响的工人立即进入就业市场。在这种竞争中，他说：“你有什么机会？”

像科达这样灰心丧气的求职者至少目前已经放弃找工作，他们属于经济学家所说的令人担忧的趋势的一部分：自世纪之交以来，由于人口老龄化和进入劳动力市场的年轻人减少，劳动力参与率一直呈下降趋势。

6 月份，25 岁​​至 54 岁工人的黄金年龄劳动力参与率出现自 1976 年 6 月以来最大单月跌幅（不包括 Covid-19 大流行）。据圣路易斯联储数据，5 月至 6 月期间，大约有 72 万人停止工作或寻找工作。专门研究中产阶级经济学的海军联邦信用合作社首席经济学家希瑟·朗 (Heather Long) 表示，离开劳动力市场的人既有男性也有女性，大多数年龄在 25 岁至 34 岁之间。

与此同时，长期失业率仍然居高不下。根据美国劳工统计局的数据，6 月份，超过 190 万美国人，即大约四分之一的失业者，失业但仍在寻找工作超过六个月。持续的低雇佣、低解雇的就业市场可能会让找工作变得更加困难，并导致更多的人完全退出劳动力市场。

朗表示，关于退出劳动力市场的官方数据可能会在未来几个月内向下修正，并指出一个月的峰值表明在最初的数据提取中“有些事情不太对劲”。但劳动力参与率下降仍然加剧了美国劳动力经济似乎失衡且几乎看不到解决方案的局面。

促使人们退出劳动力市场的因素不仅仅包括工人支付日常必需品的费用，还包括阻碍职业发展轨迹和影响长期退休储蓄。

心理健康压力因素正在迫使一些人放弃求职：“我没有精力”

经济学家表示，一些复合因素可能会降低劳动力参与率，例如退休工人的外流和美国移民的减少。朗说，一些在职父母，尤其是年幼孩子的妈妈和残疾人可能会受到淘汰，因为他们面临着对远程或灵活工作机会的更多竞争，而这些机会如今很难获得。

心理健康也可能发挥一定作用。科达说，在与妻子交谈后，他在六月份停止了找工作，因为妻子注意到这个令人厌烦的过程让他的心情变得糟糕。

罗格斯大学赫尔德里奇劳动力发展中心主任卡尔·范·霍恩 (Carl Van Horn) 6 月份对 CNBC 表示：“除了家庭成员或亲密朋友的死亡之外，[失业]是人们面临的最具破坏性的事情之一。”

根据 Resume Genius 4 月份对 1,000 名活跃的美国求职者进行的调查，大约一半的求职者表示，由于拒绝、缺乏回应、经济压力和动力减弱，求职对他们的心理健康产生了负面影响。

与此同时，雇主也倾向于质疑简历上的差距，这可能会让求职者寻找工作的时间越长就越难找到工作。

科达表示，他在求职期间的心理健康状况虽然令人沮丧，但受到不温不火的反应的影响较小，因为他的家人一直在积极储蓄。他和他的妻子仍然全职从事人力资源工作，一直在努力争取提前退休。尽管他们现在正在动用这些积蓄，但科达表示，随着他们减少外出就餐、庭院维护和房屋清洁服务，家人可以更好地承受他的中断。

其他人就没那么幸运了。海娜和其他一些来自中国内蒙古的人一样只有一个名字，她说，在一次疲惫不堪的求职过程给她的心理健康带来压力后，她只能依靠家人。

这位 33 岁的女士于 2025 年 11 月被解雇，当时她的营销分析职位被解雇，当时她住在纽约。在接下来的几个月里，她安排了面试，甚至获得了一些工作机会，但她表示，找到新雇主来满足她的 H-1B 签证需求一直很困难。 （雇主通常必须代表雇员申请签证转移，申请费、处理费和律师费之间的费用高达数千美元。）

5月，海娜停止了在美国的求职，回到内蒙古与家人团聚。从那时起，她说她又感觉更像自己了。海纳说，找工作就像“起起落落的过山车”：“如果你一个月前遇见我，我会是一个完全不同的人。我没有精力。”

海娜目前与父母住在一起，这意味着她的开支很少，她说，自八年前离开美国以来，她第一次很长时间待在家里。

“我只是想真正利用这一刻与家人共度时光，并认真思考我想做什么，”她说。

有些人回到学校是为了寻求优势：“我需要把它收拾好”
